extracted.intended_audience: journalists, journalism students, newsroom data teams and anyone learning data-driven reporting
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive standards for producing data-driven journalism: what it is, the skills/tools required, the multi-step workflow (find, clean, visualize, publish, distribute, measure), considerations about data quality and trust, and taxonomies of project/story types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose: data-driven journalism definition and goal
rubrics_metrics.description: Data journalism is 'journalism based on the filtering and analysis of large data sets for the purpose of creating or elevating a news story.' Telling stories based on the data is the primary goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The approach should produce stories that are verifiable, trustworthy, relevant and easy to remember; visualizations and storytelling elements are used to illustrate what the findings mean for people affected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find: searching for and obtaining data
rubrics_metrics.description: Find: Searching for data on the web — obtain data from governmental databases (e.g. data.gov, data.gov.uk, World Bank API), Freedom of Information requests, scrapers for webpages, OCR for PDFs, or crowd-sourced/public contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of tools and sources: APIs, FOI requests, scrapers (WebScraper, Import.io, QuickCode, OutWit Hub), OCR software. Note national differences in openness and usable formats; sometimes data must be created by the public through crowdsourcing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Digging deep / data acquisition workflow
rubrics_metrics.description: A core workflow element: 'digging deep into data by scraping, cleansing and structuring it' (Mirko Lorenz).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This may require specialized technical skills and tools to extract and structure raw data prior to analysis (see Find and Clean criteria).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clean: data cleaning, structuring and transformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Clean: process to filter and transform data, preparation for visualization — datasets often need cleaning, structuring and transformation (rows/columns, too many datapoints, format issues).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tools mentioned: OpenRefine, Data Wrangler, Google Spreadsheets. Cleaning is necessary to make data suitable for analysis and visualization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filter / Interrogate / Mine data
rubrics_metrics.description: Filter: mining for specific information — interrogate the data to find the story (understanding of jargon and statistics is necessary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This phase requires statistical understanding and subject-matter knowledge to interpret patterns; Paul Bradshaw describes 'interrogated' data as a distinct phase after finding data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualize: create meaningful visual representations
rubrics_metrics.description: Visualize: display patterns as static or interactive visuals (graphs, charts, maps, infographics) to help readers understand significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriate libraries/tools (Many Eyes, Tableau Public, Google Fusion Tables, HTML5 canvas libraries, RGraph, numerous JavaScript libraries). Guidance includes producing meaningful and relevant visualizations rather than decorative ones; avoid visualizations that show a problem without explaining it (van Ess critique).

rubrics_metrics.name: Make a story / storytelling with data
rubrics_metrics.description: Make a story: transform findings into journalistic writing; use elements of storytelling to illustrate what the findings actually mean from the perspective of those affected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Data alone is insufficient — combine narrative and interpretation so outputs are not 'in orbit with the laws of good story telling.' Good productions should allow both personal drill-downs and big-picture context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish: integrate visuals and attach data to stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Publish: integrate visualizations in articles, embed interactive elements, and attach the underlying data to stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options range from attaching datasets to single stories to building single dossiers or special pages that aggregate multiple visualizations and articles; many CMSs are optimized for single posts, so specials may need custom coding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribute / provide access to data
rubrics_metrics.description: Distribute: enable access to data and visualizations across devices and make datasets discoverable so others can investigate and reuse them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide links to datasets used (especially when gained from Open Data), use platforms/marketplaces (Buzzdata, ScraperWiki, Timetric, Help Me Investigate) to share and foster community investigation; enabling reuse can start new cycles of interrogation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure: track usage and impact ethically
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure: track how often a dataset or visualization is viewed to assess impact, but tracking should avoid intrusive data collection that may be problematic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-intrusive options include lightweight trackers like PixelPing (ProPublica/DocumentCloud project). Be cautious about collecting user data beyond readers' control for marketing or other uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data quality assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Critically examine data quality: many datasets have omissions, misleading entries or are in unusable formats (e.g., PDFs); data quality examination is an important part of data-driven journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If data are poor or withheld, the story can itself be about data quality or institutional refusals to provide data. Explicitly document limitations, gaps and provenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust and ethical value proposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Data-driven journalism should aim to 'move from attention to trust' by becoming a trusted data hub that verifies and explains facts, since trust is a scarce resource in the digital era.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Building trust includes transparency about data sources, methods, and avoiding exploitative tracking; aim for verifiability and relevance to audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skills and tools required
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical skills: finding data may require MySQL or Python; interrogation requires understanding of statistics and jargon; visualization and presentation often use open-source tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teams often include or benefit from data specialists; many news organizations have dedicated 'data teams' producing visualizations for newsrooms (examples: Reuters, ProPublica, La Nacion, The Guardian).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of open data and open-source tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Many data-driven stories begin with open data and make use of open-source tools for analysis and visualization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible publish or link to the data and prefer open tools to enable reproducibility and wider use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Layered productions and personalization (drill down / zoom out)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good data-driven productions have different layers: allow users to 'drill down' to personalized relevant details and to 'zoom out' to get the big picture (van Ess).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design interactive outputs that support both individualized exploration and overarching context; avoid products that merely 'show the problem' without explaining it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigative data journalism suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigative data journalism combines data practices with investigative reporting and can handle large textual or financial datasets and occasionally 'not-so-open' (secret or leaked) data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Projects can assume an investigative role when analyzing non-public or complex datasets; examples include Wikileaks-driven projects and large leak analyses (Afghan War Diary, Offshore Leaks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxonomy of project/story types (form and content)
rubrics_metrics.description: Several taxonomies classify data journalism projects by form and required interpretation level: Knight's list (number pullquote, static map, list and timelines, table, graphs and charts, dynamic map, textual analysis, infographics); Simon Rogers' five types (By just the facts, Data-based news stories, Local data telling stories, Analysis and background, Deep dive investigations); Martha Kang's seven story types (narrate change over time; start big and drill down; start small and zoom out; highlight contrasts; explore the intersection; dissect the factors; profile the outliers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these taxonomies to select the appropriate form for your findings and audience; the taxonomy informs the level of interpretation and presentation required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation-based taxonomy (transmissional/consultational/conversational)
rubrics_metrics.description: Veglis and Bratsas propose a taxonomy based on presentation method: hierarchy from articles with just numbers, with tables, with visualizations (interactive and non-interactive); interactive visualizations can be transmissional, consultational, or conversational.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose presentation mode according to audience needs: transmissional (push), consultational (allow queries), conversational (two-way interaction/community engagement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility and transparency: attach/source data
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should provide a link to the data they used for others to investigate (particularly when insights were gained from Open Data).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attaching data aids reproducibility, invites further analysis, and supports trust; consider publishing datasets, methods and code where possible.
